title: Could We Build an Entire City That Floats?

publication.reason: Revision c-r2, locked by the owner with its claims approved (2026-11-08); visuals in internal production, not approved for publication.

beats.narration: 10,000 people, with homes, schools, a clinic, parks, and streets to walk along. And not one of them is standing on land.
beats.visual_goal: Establishing aerial of the finished illustrative district in its sheltered bay, the quay in the foreground; a slow push toward the homes; NOTE 'Illustrative design'

beats.narration: Could we design a city like this, one that floats, stays where we put it, and keeps working? Let's treat it as a design problem, and solve it one step at a time.
beats.visual_goal: The push-in continues over the homes, no claim on screen

beats.narration: Floating neighborhoods are not science fiction. In Amsterdam, a floating neighborhood called Schoonschip is home to 46 households, a little over 100 people. Much larger designs exist on paper. One, for 12,000 people off the coast of Busan in South Korea, was unveiled in 2022, and when we checked in November 2026, its architects still listed it as in design.
beats.visual_goal: Scale card: Schoonschip (built, 46 households, schematic squares, no photograph) beside OCEANIX Busan (proposed 2022, three linked platforms, schematic); 'Architects' project page, Nov 2026: In Design'

elements.text: built · 46 households · a little over 100 people
Architects' project page, Nov 2026: In Design

beats.narration: So let's take our city apart, and build it back, one problem at a time.
beats.visual_goal: The district comes apart system by system (breakwater, moorings, utilities and routes, link-spans, buildings, platforms) until one empty platform remains

beats.narration: Problem one: how does something this heavy float at all? Take a block of concrete. As a solid lump, it sinks: concrete is more than twice as dense as seawater. Shape the same concrete into a hollow box, 40 meters on each side, and it floats.
beats.visual_goal: Section: a block holding the hull's concrete appears at the surface and sinks to the seabed; the same concrete as a hollow 40 m box then settles at its calculated draft (hull only)

annotations.text: Hull only, 40 m box: draft ≈ 1.62 m

beats.narration: It floats because it pushes water out of the way, and the water it pushes aside weighs as much as the platform. Every ton we add needs roughly one more cubic meter of water pushed aside.
beats.visual_goal: Section of the first platform (three storeys): the water the hull pushes aside lights up below the waterline

annotations.text: 1 t added ≈ 1 m³ more water pushed aside
Illustrative design, section through the middle

beats.narration: Real floating homes work exactly this way. The Schoonschip houses stand on concrete floats. The heaviest weighs around 340 to 350 metric tons, so it pushes aside roughly as many cubic meters of canal water: a cube about 7 meters on each side.
beats.visual_goal: Schematic section of a floating home on its concrete float; '340–350 t'; the water it pushes aside as a cube about 7 m on each side, two 1.8 m figures for scale

elements.text: a cube about 7 m on each side

beats.narration: Our first platform, in this illustrative design, carries four blocks of three-story homes. Altogether it weighs about 4,800 tons, and floats about 3 meters deep. And here's the surprise: more than half of that weight is the concrete hull itself.
beats.visual_goal: The first platform in section (three storeys): seen at an angle, then square on; the draft reads against the water; the buildings ghost and the concrete hull lights up: more than half of the weight

annotations.text: Illustrative design, section through the middle

beats.narration: Now add a fourth story. The platform settles about a third of a meter deeper, and the freeboard, the part of the hull above the water, shrinks from about a meter to about 70 centimeters.
beats.visual_goal: Square-on section: a fourth storey arrives; the platform settles by the calculated 0.33 m; the gold freeboard bar (above the water) shrinks from 1.04 to 0.71 m, close on the east wall

annotations.text: +1 story, same load per m² of floor

beats.narration: One fix is to make the hull half a meter deeper. That adds about 100 tons of concrete, 4% more, and brings the freeboard back to about a meter and 15 centimeters. Lighter buildings would be another way.
beats.visual_goal: Same section: close on the bottom corner, the walls and bulkheads grow 0.5 m (gold) as the bottom moves down; then the deck rises to the calculated freeboard 1.15 m

beats.narration: Will it tip over? Move 100 tons out toward the edge, and in this example the platform tilts by less than half a degree. But a small tilt under a shifted load tells us very little about how it will move in waves. Floating is only the first problem.
beats.visual_goal: The same platform whole (four storeys, deeper hull), seen square on: the front buildings ghost, a 100 t block slides 15 m toward the edge, and the platform tilts by the calculated angle (true scale, barely visible)

beats.narration: Let's go back to the three-story version. A platform like this holds about 50 people. For 10,000, we need a lot of them. So why not simply join them all into one enormous slab?
beats.visual_goal: Back to the three-storey design: the fourth storey fades and the deck returns to its first freeboard; then four copies are towed in around a small basin

beats.narration: Look at two identical platforms carrying different buildings, one with two stories and one with four. Floating on their own, their decks would sit about 66 centimeters apart in height. So different loads add a demand on whatever connects them. In this design, the walkways between platforms are hinged, so they can follow the difference. Adding ballast to even out the decks would be another option.
beats.visual_goal: Side elevation of two identical platforms with two and four storeys at their own drafts; close on the 0.66 m step between the decks; a hinged walkway arrives and spans it (no part shown failing)

annotations.text: Another option: ballast to even out the decks

beats.narration: Connections are where engineers expect trouble. A 2026 research agenda lists stress concentrations on connectors among the challenges of large floating developments. One concept study links its modules flexibly, and spaces them far enough apart not to collide, because on flexible moorings they are expected to move sideways quite a lot.
beats.visual_goal: Close-up of one joint: the gap, the hinged walkway, the flexible utility link and the fenders, each lit as it is named (conceptual geometry, not sized)

beats.narration: How many platforms would 10,000 people need? Say each resident needs about 40 square meters of floor: thirty for their home, and ten for a share of schools, shops and services. That's about thirty-three hectares of platform: about 200 platforms like our first one, with hundreds of connections between them.
beats.visual_goal: One plan diagram (continues into B16): 40 m cells appear until about 33 ha are covered (209 cells); the joints between them light up as they are counted

beats.narration: Bigger platforms mean fewer connections. At 100 meters on a side, 34 would do, but each would weigh about 30,000 tons, to build, launch and tow. Even the Schoonschip floats were too big for the dry docks of traditional houseboat builders, and were cast on the quay instead. Our district uses 60-meter platforms with three-story homes, 93 of them: a middle choice for this illustration, not an optimum.
beats.visual_goal: Same diagram as B15: the cells regroup into 34 platforms of 100 m (fewer joints; about 30,000 t each), the Schoonschip quay note, then settle on the district's 93 platforms of 60 m around their lagoon

elements.text: Schoonschip's floats: cast on the quay,
too big for houseboat dry docks
a middle choice for this illustration,

beats.narration: And all of this sits on water that never keeps still. Each platform rises and falls on its own, and every gap and hinge between them has to cope.
beats.visual_goal: Five platforms rise, fall and tilt out of step; the gaps open and close and the walkways follow one side (conceptual motion, labelled)
beats.motion_label: Conceptual motion visualization — not a hydrodynamic simulation

annotations.text: Conceptual motion visualization — not a hydrodynamic simulation

beats.narration: People living on the water feel it. Floating homes in the Netherlands can rock in storms, or when large cruise ships pass, and one Amsterdam resident feels it most on her upper floor.
beats.visual_goal: Floating home in section rocking (storm, passing cruise ship); the upper floor marked; source line

elements.text: felt most on the upper floor

beats.narration: Very large platforms don't only move. They bend, and predicting exactly how is still an open research problem.
beats.visual_goal: A long platform drawn flat, then bending (exaggerated, conceptual); 'an open research problem'

elements.text: How exactly? An open research problem

beats.narration: So the first fix is where you build. A 2026 concept study looks for sea areas with limited fetch, near a gulf, a strait or an archipelago, where waves stay moderate. That's why our city sits in a sheltered bay, connected to an existing city on shore.
beats.visual_goal: Two schematic coasts: open coast with long fetch vs a sheltered bay with limited fetch; the district placed in the bay beside the city's quay

elements.text: our city: sheltered, connected to the shore

beats.narration: The second fix is the layout. Following one concept study, homes go in the middle, and functions that can tolerate more motion form the outer ring. Where the bay opens to the sea, a breakwater reduces the waves. But a floating breakwater may not be enough against longer waves from the open sea, and how much wave energy passes behind one is still hard to predict.
beats.visual_goal: From the plan to an aerial view: inner homes light, then the outer ring of services; the breakwater arrives on the open side; NOTE 'reduces waves, does not remove storm risk'

annotations.text: Reduces waves; does not remove storm risk

beats.narration: Something also has to hold the city in place. Floating homes in the Netherlands are fixed to the shore, often resting against steel poles.
beats.visual_goal: Low view of the neighbourhood: the water ghosts and the steel piles beneath light up

beats.narration: Water levels rise and fall, and a floating platform rises and falls with them, sliding along its poles. In our scenario, the water level can change by about 2 meters, so the bridges to shore need hinges: including changes in loading, the slope of a 25-meter bridge changes by about 3 degrees either way.
beats.visual_goal: Elevation at true slope: quay, shore hinge, a 25 m link-span to a platform on its pile; the water and the platform rise and fall, the bridge turns on its hinge; '2 m water level (assumed) + loading; about 2.8° either way'

elements.text: Water level and the hinged bridge (illustrative)
25 m bridge: slope changes ≈ 2.8° either way
shore hinge at the middle of the range

beats.narration: Further out, the water is deeper, and piles give way to mooring lines anchored in the seabed. Deeper water means longer lines, deeper anchors, and higher costs. The seabed itself shapes the design, and the bill.
beats.visual_goal: Same neighbourhood with the water ghosted: the piles fade and mooring lines to anchors on the seabed take their place; lines and anchors light (conceptual mooring, not sized)

beats.narration: So it floats, and it stays put. But is it a city yet? Fade out the buildings, and the city's other half appears.
beats.visual_goal: Close to the quay: the buildings ghost and the city's other half appears: power, water and wastewater lines along the bridges and through the district

beats.narration: Power first: at Schoonschip, 46 households share a single connection to the national grid, with solar panels, a battery in every house, and a smart grid between them. Floating doesn't mean off-grid.
beats.visual_goal: Schematic: 46 homes on the water, one cable to the grid on land; solar panels, a battery per house, a smart grid between them; 'Floating ≠ off-grid'

beats.narration: Wastewater is separated there too: gray water from showers and washing machines, black water from toilets. Connecting floating homes to sewers on land takes extra infrastructure, such as waterproof cables and pumps. In our city, wastewater is pumped ashore along the bridges, and drinking water comes back the same way.
beats.visual_goal: One bridge to the quay, close: the bridge deck ghosts, and the wastewater line beneath it, then the drinking-water line, light as they are named

beats.narration: Transport, fire and medical services, and food all follow the same logic. A large floating development has to connect sewage, power and roads to land, or develop alternatives of its own, and our city connects.
beats.visual_goal: The whole district: boat landings for fire and rescue, the emergency routes to the bridges, the utility lines, then the bridges themselves light in turn

beats.narration: Everything so far assumed sheltered water close to a city. So what happens if we tow it out to sea?
beats.visual_goal: The same district alone on the open sea (counterfactual), seen from above

annotations.text: Counterfactual: the same district at open sea

beats.narration: Longer waves arrive, and a floating breakwater may not be enough against them. Below the surface, the seabed drops away, so mooring lines get longer and anchors deeper.
beats.visual_goal: Long conceptual swell passes along the breakwater (labelled); the water ghosts and the long mooring lines to deep anchors light
beats.motion_label: Conceptual motion visualization — not a hydrodynamic simulation

annotations.text: Conceptual motion visualization — not a hydrodynamic simulation

beats.narration: Further from shore, cables, pipes and supply ships can still reach the city, but every link becomes longer and more exposed.
beats.visual_goal: From above with the water ghosted: three cables and pipes run along the seabed toward a shore beyond the frame, and light

annotations.text: Links to a shore beyond the frame, not sized

beats.narration: And if we also asked the city to supply itself, as one 2026 offshore concept does, it would need its own systems for energy, water and food. In that study, growing food alone accounts for nearly half of the city's estimated energy use.
beats.visual_goal: An added condition: three systems (energy, water, food) appear; a bar shows food production as nearly half of the study's estimated energy use; 'one concept study's estimate'

elements.text: food production: ≈ 48% of the estimated energy use
Autonomy is an extra choice, not a consequence of floating

beats.narration: That study also uses a different kind of hull: semi-submersible platforms, with the deck raised above the sea on columns, behind a floating barrier. Offshore isn't the same city moved further out. It's a different design.
beats.visual_goal: Our box pontoon, then beside it a semi-submersible module rises into place: pontoons under the water (ghosted), columns through the surface, the deck raised above the sea (schematic of a 2026 concept study)

annotations.text: Schematic of a 2026 concept study's module

beats.narration: Some difficulties remain wherever we build. Concrete in seawater needs watching: chlorides can corrode the steel reinforcement, and, according to a 2026 study, there are no dedicated standards for floating cities yet.
beats.visual_goal: Low on the hull's side: the water ghosts and the concrete below the waterline lights (no damage shown)

annotations.text: Illustrative: inspection zone, no damage shown

beats.narration: Large floating developments change the light, shade and water movement beneath them, effects that researchers say still need study, and they expect the impact on local ecology to be far larger than that of small developments.
beats.visual_goal: Below the district with the water ghosted: the platforms' shade on the seabed (illustrative)

annotations.text: Shade illustrative; effects still need study

beats.narration: And who gets to use the water? How districts like this fit into planning law is not yet known, and researchers warn they could end up serving the wealthy, and fencing off water that used to be public.
beats.visual_goal: Two waterfront edges: a public path along the water vs a private, fenced edge; 'planning law: not yet known'

elements.text: Who gets to use the water?

beats.narration: And what would it cost? We do not yet have a reliable cost estimate for this design. The one published framework we found is preliminary, and covers only flotation and energy. Compared with land, floating structures can follow the water level, and can be moved or reused, but they trade a fixed foundation for moorings, connections and ongoing maintenance.
beats.visual_goal: Two columns, no numbers: what floating gives (follows the water, movable) and what it costs (moorings, connections, maintenance); 'no reliable cost estimate for this design yet'

elements.text: No reliable cost estimate for this design yet
the one published framework: preliminary; flotation and energy only

beats.narration: From one platform to a district, every part we added answers a question we had to ask.
beats.visual_goal: From one platform to the whole district: the camera pulls back while the systems we added light in turn (walkways, moorings, breakwater, utilities)

beats.narration: So, could we build an entire city that floats? Small floating neighborhoods, connected to the shore in sheltered water, already exist.
beats.visual_goal: Verdict, tier 1 of 3: small floating neighbourhoods, sheltered and connected: already exist

elements.text: Could we build an entire city that floats?
Small floating neighbourhoods, sheltered and connected

beats.narration: A connected district for 10,000 people, in a sheltered bay, built step by step, may be possible under the right conditions. But how very large platforms bend, how their connections hold up, and what they would cost are still open questions. And the one project of that size we checked is still listed as in design.
beats.visual_goal: Verdict, tier 2 of 3: a connected district in a sheltered bay, possible under the right conditions; the open questions; 'the one project of that size we checked: still listed as in design'

elements.text: Could we build an entire city that floats?

beats.narration: A city far out at sea, especially one that has to supply itself, remains much more speculative.
beats.visual_goal: Verdict, tier 3 of 3: a city far out at sea that supplies itself: much more speculative

beats.narration: Our arithmetic shows what it takes for a platform to float. Whether a whole district works depends on the site, and on every other system we added.
beats.visual_goal: Closing aerial of the district (the opening view), a slow push
